newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico govt sets new econ pact with labor, business.
newsitem.headline: Mexico govt sets new econ pact with labor, business.

text.p: The Mexican goverment was set to sign a new economic pact for 1997 on Saturday with business and labor representatives, officials and news reports said.
A spokesman for the office of President Ernesto Zedillo said the pact, set annually since 1987, would be signed during the day at the presidential residence of Los Pinos in Mexico City.
Radio station Radio Red reported that final details of the accord were thrashed out at an all-night meeting and that it would be signed at around 1.30 p.m. (1830 GMT).
Radio Red and Reforma newspaper both said the pact would include an increase of between 16 percent and 18 percent in the minimum wage from December.
It would also leave in place the current free flotation of the Mexican peso, they said.
Gasoline and electricity prices were also set to rise by about 20 percent over 1997, probably by monthly increments after a rise of around eight percent in December, they added.
The government inflation target for 1997 is about 15 percent.
Officials said Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz and Central Bank Gov. Miguel Mancera would announce more details of the pact on Sunday morning.
The annual economic pact changes its name every year but is universally known as the Pacto.
Last year's tripartite accord, constructed to help Mexico overcome a deep recession following the December 1994 peso crash, was officially called the Alliance for Economic Recovery.

The Pacto was instituted by former President Miguel de la Madrid in 1987 to help rein in inflation and lay the groundwork for economic growth, and was continued by his successor Carlos Salinas de Gortari.
